title: Isaiah 6 — The throne-room vision and the prophet's commission

verdicts.reasoning: Re-parsed MT reads the consonantal אֶת־אֲדֹנָי (Adonai, not the Tetragrammaton) and רָם וְנִשָּׂא agreeing with masc.sg. כִּסֵּא; 'the Lord... a throne, high and lifted up... the hem of his robe filled the temple' is the consensus construal (throne-attachment, not the independent Isa 57:15 God-attachment), and the YHWH/Adonai typographic distinction is a defensible textual-fidelity choice.

citations: Joines, 'Winged Serpents in Isaiah's Inaugural Vision', JBL 86 (1967) 410-415
verdicts.reasoning: MT שְׂרָפִים transliterated 'seraphim'; the beings have face/feet/wings/voice and act as courtiers, so the 'fiery/flying serpents' reading (śārāp̄ of Num 21:6) is rightly declined for the throne-vision and confined to commentary — no serpent, craft, or sky-attendant reading surfaced in the line.

Threefold קָדוֹשׁ preserved as 'Holy, holy, holy' (not collapsed to an intensive superlative); 'YHWH of hosts' and 'his glory' hold the standard surface with the ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ/kᵉḇôḏô lens confined to commentary; the literal word-order 'the fullness of the whole earth is his glory' (kᵉḇôḏô as predicate) is a defensible construal of מְלֹא כָל־הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ alongside the smoother 'the whole earth is full of his glory.'
MT re-parsed; 'the foundations of the thresholds' (JPS) for אַמּוֹת הַסִּפִּים and the durative 'kept filling' for the yiqtol יִמָּלֵא are accurate; a lens-free scene-setting verse.

citations: BDB s.v. דמה II 'be cut off, ruined'; HALOT s.v. דמה
verdicts.reasoning: נִדְמֵיתִי is a genuine root-crux (dmh 'be cut off/ruined' vs dmm 'be silenced'); 'I am undone' follows the majority reading grounded by the following seeing-the-deity clause (Exod 33:20; Judg 13:22), with the dmm minority flagged in commentary; 'the King, YHWH of hosts' holds the standard titles.

paragraphs.text: בִּשְׁנַת־מוֹת֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ וָאֶרְאֶ֧ה אֶת־אֲדֹנָ֛י יֹשֵׁ֥ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֖א רָ֣ם וְנִשָּׂ֑א וְשׁוּלָ֖יו מְלֵאִ֥ים אֶת־הַהֵיכָֽל׃

i18n.en: In the year of King Uzziah's death, I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, high and lifted up, and the hem of his robe filled the temple.
i18n.he: בִּשְׁנַת־מוֹת֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ וָאֶרְאֶ֧ה אֶת־אֲדֹנָ֛י יֹשֵׁ֥ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֖א רָ֣ם וְנִשָּׂ֑א וְשׁוּלָ֖יו מְלֵאִ֥ים אֶת־הַהֵיכָֽל׃

notes.official:
*ʾăḏōnāy* — the bare divine title “the Lord” — opens the vision, and Isaiah 6 deploys it pointedly against the Tetragrammaton: *ʾăḏōnāy* here and at the commissioning (v 8) and the lament (v 11), but *YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* in the seraphim's cry (v 3) and Isaiah's confession (v 5). The translation keeps the two distinct — “the Lord” for *ʾăḏōnāy*, “YHWH” for the Tetragrammaton — where the English “the LORD / the Lord” convention would blur them. The consonantal text reads *ʾăḏōnāy*, and scribal sensitivity around the divine names in this chapter is noted, but the received text is not emended to “YHWH.”

*rām wᵉniśśāʾ* “high and lifted up” follows and agrees with *kissēʾ* “throne,” so the pair is read as attributive to the throne (“a throne, high and lifted up”), with Wildberger (*Isaiah 1–12*, 1991) and Williamson (ICC *Isaiah 6–12*, 2018); the same word-pair describes God at Isa 57:15, but that is an independent construction.

*šûlāyw* — the hem, skirt, or train of the robe — floods the *hêḵāl*. The image is spatial and anthropomorphic: a mere hem of the seated figure's robe fills the whole hall, implying the immensity of the One enthroned (Blenkinsopp, *Isaiah 1–39*, AB 19, 2000). *hêḵāl* means both “temple” and “palace / great hall”; the translation keeps “temple” (the altar of v 6 and the year-of-Uzziah setting fix the Jerusalem sanctuary), while the word also carries the register of a sovereign's audience-hall — the setting in which a throne-court convenes and dispatches its messenger.

paragraphs.text: שְׂרָפִ֨ים עֹמְדִ֤ים ׀ מִמַּ֙עַל֙ ל֔וֹ שֵׁ֧שׁ כְּנָפַ֛יִם שֵׁ֥שׁ כְּנָפַ֖יִם לְאֶחָ֑ד בִּשְׁתַּ֣יִם ׀ יְכַסֶּ֣ה פָנָ֗יו וּבִשְׁתַּ֛יִם יְכַסֶּ֥ה רַגְלָ֖יו וּבִשְׁתַּ֥יִם יְעוֹפֵֽף׃

i18n.en: Seraphim were standing above him; each had six wings — with two he covered his face, with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.
i18n.he: שְׂרָפִ֨ים עֹמְדִ֤ים ׀ מִמַּ֙עַל֙ ל֔וֹ שֵׁ֧שׁ כְּנָפַ֛יִם שֵׁ֥שׁ כְּנָפַ֖יִם לְאֶחָ֑ד בִּשְׁתַּ֣יִם ׀ יְכַסֶּ֣ה פָנָ֗יו וּבִשְׁתַּ֛יִם יְכַסֶּ֥ה רַגְלָ֖יו וּבִשְׁתַּ֥יִם יְעוֹפֵֽף׃

notes.official:
*śᵉrāp̄îm*, from the root *śrp* “to burn,” are the “burning ones” — six-winged attendants standing above the throne. The translation transliterates “seraphim” (ASV/JPS): the term functions here as the proper name of an order of throne-beings, not as a live adjective, and “burning ones” is reserved for this note.

The rendering “fiery/flying serpents” — the *śārāp̄* of Num 21:6, Deut 8:15, Isa 14:29, 30:6, and the winged-uraeus iconography behind the seraph-figure discussed by Joines (*JBL* 86 [1967] 410–415) and Wildberger — is deliberately declined for the throne-vision: whatever the figure's iconographic prehistory, the beings of Isaiah 6 have faces, hands, feet, and voices and act as courtiers. Two wings cover the face (before the deity), two cover the “feet” (*raḡlayim*, here most likely the common euphemism), and two are for flight. These winged throne-attendants align cross-corpus with the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4, who take up the same threefold “holy” — see the central *merkavah*-tradition entry.

paragraphs.text: וְקָרָ֨א זֶ֤ה אֶל־זֶה֙ וְאָמַ֔ר קָד֧וֹשׁ ׀ קָד֛וֹשׁ קָד֖וֹשׁ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת מְלֹ֥א כָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ כְּבוֹדֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And one called to another and said: “Holy, holy, holy is YHWH of hosts; the fullness of the whole earth is his glory.”
i18n.he: וְקָרָ֨א זֶ֤ה אֶל־זֶה֙ וְאָמַ֔ר קָד֧וֹשׁ ׀ קָד֛וֹשׁ קָד֖וֹשׁ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֑וֹת מְלֹ֥א כָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ כְּבוֹדֽוֹ׃

notes.official:
The seraphim's threefold *qādôš qādôš qādôš* — the Trisagion — is preserved as the threefold “Holy, holy, holy,” not collapsed to an intensive superlative. Hebrew can mark the superlative by repetition, but the threefold form is the structural feature that carries into the reception tradition and is preserved as such. This is the source-text of the cross-corpus Isa 6:3 → Rev 4:8 → the Jewish Kedushah and the Christian Sanctus; the handling is governed by the central Trisagion entry (see the editorial report for the ISA-6:3 wiring).

*YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* “YHWH of hosts” is kept as the standard title. *ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* “armies, hosts” is read by Mullen (*The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature*, 1980) and Cross (*Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic*, 1973) as the heavenly host — the assembled army of divine beings YHWH commands — which is precisely the company attending the throne in this vision; that reading is stated here rather than by altering the fixed epithet.

*mᵉlōʾ ḵol-hā-ʾāreṣ kᵉḇôḏô* is rendered in its literal word order, “the fullness of the whole earth is his glory,” keeping *kᵉḇôḏô* as the clause's predicate. *kāḇôḏ* (root *kbd* “be heavy”) is the weighty, radiant, quasi-physical presence-manifestation of the deity — the same phenomenon the smoke filling the house dramatizes in v 4 (cf. the *kavod*-tradition of Exod 40, 1 Kgs 8, Ezek 1). The suffixed form here differs grammatically from the construct *kᵉḇôḏ-YHWH* of Ezekiel; the shared presence-vocabulary is the point.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּנֻ֙עוּ֙ אַמּ֣וֹת הַסִּפִּ֔ים מִקּ֖וֹל הַקּוֹרֵ֑א וְהַבַּ֖יִת יִמָּלֵ֥א עָשָֽׁן׃

i18n.en: And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of the one who called, and the house kept filling with smoke.
i18n.he: וַיָּנֻ֙עוּ֙ אַמּ֣וֹת הַסִּפִּ֔ים מִקּ֖וֹל הַקּוֹרֵ֑א וְהַבַּ֖יִת יִמָּלֵ֥א עָשָֽׁן׃

paragraphs.text: וָאֹמַ֞ר אֽוֹי־לִ֣י כִֽי־נִדְמֵ֗יתִי כִּ֣י אִ֤ישׁ טְמֵֽא־שְׂפָתַ֙יִם֙ אָנֹ֔כִי וּבְתוֹךְ֙ עַם־טְמֵ֣א שְׂפָתַ֔יִם אָנֹכִ֖י יוֹשֵׁ֑ב כִּ֗י אֶת־הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת רָא֥וּ עֵינָֽי׃

i18n.en: And I said: “Woe is me, for I am undone! For I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips — for my eyes have seen the King, YHWH of hosts.”
i18n.he: וָאֹמַ֞ר אֽוֹי־לִ֣י כִֽי־נִדְמֵ֗יתִי כִּ֣י אִ֤ישׁ טְמֵֽא־שְׂפָתַ֙יִם֙ אָנֹ֔כִי וּבְתוֹךְ֙ עַם־טְמֵ֣א שְׂפָתַ֔יִם אָנֹכִ֖י יוֹשֵׁ֑ב כִּ֗י אֶת־הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת רָא֥וּ עֵינָֽי׃

notes.official:
*niḏmêṯî* “I am undone” is a root-crux: from *dmh* “be cut off, ruined” (hence “I am undone / doomed”) or from *dmm* “be silenced, struck dumb.” The translation reads *dmh*, the majority sense, because the ground Isaiah gives is “for my eyes have seen the King” — the lethal danger of seeing the deity (Exod 33:20; Judg 13:22), a fear of destruction rather than of muteness. The “struck dumb” reading would chime with the “unclean lips” motif and is a live alternative, noted here but not placed in the text.

*ha-meleḵ* “the King,” in apposition to *YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ*, titles the enthroned figure — the royal designation the whole scene sustains. Isaiah's “woe” turns on having physically seen the King: the vision presses the tradition that no one sees God and lives (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp), which is why the lips — the organ of a prophet's speech and the seat of his declared uncleanness — must be purged before he can be sent.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֣עָף אֵלַ֗י אֶחָד֙ מִן־הַשְּׂרָפִ֔ים וּבְיָד֖וֹ רִצְפָּ֑ה בְּמֶ֨לְקַחַ֔יִם לָקַ֖ח מֵעַ֥ל הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ׃

i18n.en: Then one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken with tongs from upon the altar.
i18n.he: וַיָּ֣עָף אֵלַ֗י אֶחָד֙ מִן־הַשְּׂרָפִ֔ים וּבְיָד֖וֹ רִצְפָּ֑ה בְּמֶ֨לְקַחַ֔יִם לָקַ֖ח מֵעַ֥ל הַמִּזְבֵּֽחַ׃

notes.official: One of the *śᵉrāp̄îm* brings a *riṣpāh* — a live, glowing coal or hot stone (cf. 1 Kgs 19:6) — lifted from the altar with tongs (*melqāḥayim*), too hot to hold in the hand. The purgation is enacted with fire drawn from the sanctuary altar: the same burning that names the seraphim (“burning ones”) becomes the agent that cleanses the prophet's mouth.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּגַּ֣ע עַל־פִּ֔י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּ֛ה נָגַ֥ע זֶ֖ה עַל־שְׂפָתֶ֑יךָ וְסָ֣ר עֲוֺנֶ֔ךָ וְחַטָּאתְךָ֖ תְּכֻפָּֽר׃

i18n.en: He touched it to my mouth and said: “Behold, this has touched your lips; your iniquity is removed, and your sin is atoned for.”
i18n.he: וַיַּגַּ֣ע עַל־פִּ֔י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר הִנֵּ֛ה נָגַ֥ע זֶ֖ה עַל־שְׂפָתֶ֑יךָ וְסָ֣ר עֲוֺנֶ֔ךָ וְחַטָּאתְךָ֖ תְּכֻפָּֽר׃

notes.official: The coal touches Isaiah's lips and two purgation-verbs follow: *sār* “your iniquity is removed” and *tᵉḵuppār* (Pual of *kpr*) “your sin is atoned for / purged.” The *kpr* vocabulary is the priestly language of wiping-away or covering sin; here the altar-coal performs on the prophet's lips a cultic purgation the priesthood otherwise effects by blood and fire, consecrating the “unclean lips” for the commission that immediately follows.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶשְׁמַ֞ע אֶת־ק֤וֹל אֲדֹנָי֙ אֹמֵ֔ר אֶת־מִ֥י אֶשְׁלַ֖ח וּמִ֣י יֵֽלֶךְ־לָ֑נוּ וָאֹמַ֖ר הִנְנִ֥י שְׁלָחֵֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And I said: “Here am I; send me.”
i18n.he: וָאֶשְׁמַ֞ע אֶת־ק֤וֹל אֲדֹנָי֙ אֹמֵ֔ר אֶת־מִ֥י אֶשְׁלַ֖ח וּמִ֣י יֵֽלֶךְ־לָ֑נוּ וָאֹמַ֖ר הִנְנִ֥י שְׁלָחֵֽנִי׃

notes.official:
Isaiah hears *ʾăḏōnāy* (“the Lord”) ask “Whom shall I send, and who will go *lānû* — for us?” The switch from the singular “I send” to the first-person-plural “for us” is the classic divine-council crux, alongside Gen 1:26 (*naʿăśeh* “let us make”), Gen 3:22 (“like one of us”), and Gen 11:7 (*nērᵉḏāh* “let us go down”). The translation preserves both numbers literally — “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” — without committing the line to a reading; the plural *lānû* is grammatically explicit and is rendered as such.

On the reading of the plural, the modern scholarly consensus (Mullen, *The Divine Council*, 1980; Cross, *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic*, 1973) is that the deity speaks as the enthroned head of the heavenly assembly convened in this very vision — the seraphim and the “hosts” of v 3 — deliberating and dispatching a messenger from within the council; this is the reading the Wheel of Heaven lens develops as the Council of Eternals. The plural is a direct datum of the grammar; the council interpretation is an inferred reading, stated here and governed by the proposed central divine-council entry (see the editorial report), not asserted in the text. Isaiah's *hinnēnî šᵉlāḥēnî* “Here am I; send me” is the prophetic-response formula (central *hineni* entry).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֵ֥ךְ וְאָמַרְתָּ֖ לָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֑ה שִׁמְע֤וּ שָׁמ֙וֹעַ֙ וְאַל־תָּבִ֔ינוּ וּרְא֥וּ רָא֖וֹ וְאַל־תֵּדָֽעוּ׃

i18n.en: And he said: “Go, and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; and see indeed, but do not perceive.
i18n.he: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֵ֥ךְ וְאָמַרְתָּ֖ לָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֑ה שִׁמְע֤וּ שָׁמ֙וֹעַ֙ וְאַל־תָּבִ֔ינוּ וּרְא֥וּ רָא֖וֹ וְאַל־תֵּדָֽעוּ׃

notes.official: The commission opens with the doubled-infinitive intensive — *šimʿû šāmôaʿ* “hear indeed,” *ûrᵉʾû rāʾô* “see indeed” — governed by the central doubled-infinitive entry, which already lists ISA-6:9. The paradox is set at once: hear intently, yet do not understand; look hard, yet do not perceive.

paragraphs.text: הַשְׁמֵן֙ לֵב־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֔ה וְאָזְנָ֥יו הַכְבֵּ֖ד וְעֵינָ֣יו הָשַׁ֑ע פֶּן־יִרְאֶ֨ה בְעֵינָ֜יו וּבְאָזְנָ֣יו יִשְׁמָ֗ע וּלְבָב֥וֹ יָבִ֛ין וָשָׁ֖ב וְרָ֥פָא לֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Make the heart of this people fat, make its ears heavy, and smear over its eyes — lest it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and its heart understand, and it turn back and be healed.”
i18n.he: הַשְׁמֵן֙ לֵב־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֔ה וְאָזְנָ֥יו הַכְבֵּ֖ד וְעֵינָ֣יו הָשַׁ֑ע פֶּן־יִרְאֶ֨ה בְעֵינָ֜יו וּבְאָזְנָ֣יו יִשְׁמָ֗ע וּלְבָב֥וֹ יָבִ֛ין וָשָׁ֖ב וְרָ֥פָא לֽוֹ׃

notes.official:
The hardening-commission proper: three causative imperatives addressed to the prophet — *hašmēn* “make the heart of this people fat/dull,” *haḵbēḏ* “make its ears heavy,” *hāšaʿ* “smear over / shut its eyes” — with the *pen* “lest” clause, “lest it see... and turn back and be healed.” Read at face value, the prophet is commissioned to render the people insensible (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp; Williamson).

The offense of the line was felt early, and the softening options are real: the reading may be ironic — a bitter forecast of futile reception cast as a command — or resultative (“so that,” a foreseen outcome rather than an intended purpose). The Old Greek already recasts the imperatives as a statement of fact (“the heart of this people has grown dull”), the form the New Testament citations follow (Matt 13:14–15; Acts 28:26–27), and the Targum paraphrases. The translation keeps the imperatives the Hebrew actually uses; the mitigations are recorded here rather than imposed on the text.

paragraphs.text: וָאֹמַ֕ר עַד־מָתַ֖י אֲדֹנָ֑י וַיֹּ֡אמֶר עַ֣ד אֲשֶׁר֩ אִם־שָׁא֨וּ עָרִ֜ים מֵאֵ֣ין יוֹשֵׁ֗ב וּבָתִּים֙ מֵאֵ֣ין אָדָ֔ם וְהָאֲדָמָ֖ה תִּשָּׁאֶ֥ה שְׁמָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: And I said: “How long, O Lord?” And he said: “Until cities lie in ruins with no inhabitant, and houses with no one in them, and the ground is laid waste, a desolation;
i18n.he: וָאֹמַ֕ר עַד־מָתַ֖י אֲדֹנָ֑י וַיֹּ֡אמֶר עַ֣ד אֲשֶׁר֩ אִם־שָׁא֨וּ עָרִ֜ים מֵאֵ֣ין יוֹשֵׁ֗ב וּבָתִּים֙ מֵאֵ֣ין אָדָ֔ם וְהָאֲדָמָ֖ה תִּשָּׁאֶ֥ה שְׁמָמָֽה׃

paragraphs.text: וְרִחַ֥ק יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־הָאָדָ֑ם וְרַבָּ֥ה הָעֲזוּבָ֖ה בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: and YHWH has driven the people far away, and great is the forsakenness in the midst of the land.
i18n.he: וְרִחַ֥ק יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־הָאָדָ֑ם וְרַבָּ֥ה הָעֲזוּבָ֖ה בְּקֶ֥רֶב הָאָֽרֶץ׃

paragraphs.text: וְע֥וֹד בָּהּ֙ עֲשִׂ֣רִיָּ֔ה וְשָׁ֖בָה וְהָיְתָ֣ה לְבָעֵ֑ר כָּאֵלָ֣ה וְכָאַלּ֗וֹן אֲשֶׁ֤ר בְּשַׁלֶּ֙כֶת֙ מַצֶּ֣בֶת בָּ֔ם זֶ֥רַע קֹ֖דֶשׁ מַצַּבְתָּֽהּ׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And though a tenth yet remains in it, it too shall again be for burning — like the terebinth and like the oak, whose stump remains in them when they are felled; the holy seed is its stump.”
i18n.he: וְע֥וֹד בָּהּ֙ עֲשִׂ֣רִיָּ֔ה וְשָׁ֖בָה וְהָיְתָ֣ה לְבָעֵ֑ר כָּאֵלָ֣ה וְכָאַלּ֗וֹן אֲשֶׁ֤ר בְּשַׁלֶּ֙כֶת֙ מַצֶּ֣בֶת בָּ֔ם זֶ֥רַע קֹ֖דֶשׁ מַצַּבְתָּֽהּ׃ (פ)

notes.official:
The remnant-image and a textual crux. A “tenth” survives, yet *wᵉšāḇāh wᵉhāyᵉṯāh lᵉḇāʿēr* “it too shall again be for burning” (*bʿr* “burn, consume”) — even the remnant is subject to a further purge, “like the terebinth (*ʾēlāh*) and like the oak (*ʾallôn*)” whose *maṣṣeḇeṯ* “stump” remains *bᵉšalleḵeṯ* “when felled.”

The closing clause *zeraʿ qōḏeš maṣṣaḇtāh* “the holy seed is its stump” identifies that surviving stump with a consecrated remnant — the seed-line from which the felled people can regrow (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp; Williamson). The clause is textually contested: it is absent from the Old Greek (LXX), which many read as a later, hope-bearing addition to an otherwise unrelieved oracle of devastation. The translation retains the Masoretic clause (the project renders the MT) and discloses the LXX-minus here for the reader's audit; the remnant / holy-seed theology — a preserved seed surviving catastrophe — is developed in the commentary and the wiki, not the line.
